entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret a continuous-time system as a rule that transforms an input signal into an output signal, connecting the system-as-transformation view to later filters, circuits, differential-equation models, and system-property tests.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Systems as Signal Transformations
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the model of a continuous-time system as a rule mapping input signals to output signals so learners can identify system structure in later topics.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual data is required; this section is driven by symbolic notation and brief analogies.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Name a system as an input-to-output transformation, using both function-style notation x(t) -> y(t) and operator-style notation y(t)=T{x(t)}.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with the identity transformation y(t)=x(t) and then a scaled transform y(t)=2x(t) to show the same structure with one wrinkle.
paragraph_plan: Frame prior signal-language: what x(t), y(t), and t mean in this course context.
Define a system as the mapping that takes an input signal and returns an output signal for every t.
Introduce notation y(t)=T{x(t)} and connect T{·} to a fixed transformation rule.
Show two mini symbolic substitutions for the identity and scalar-multiple examples, emphasizing that the input is transformed rather than memorized.
Preview the lesson progression: classify what is input vs. system vs. output, then apply and recognize the same rule across examples.

sections.handoff_notes: No example or practice content is needed in this first tutorial section; keep the direct-instruction payload compact and notation-first.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing a Signal from a System
sections.learning_goal: Help learners separate symbols for signals from the system rule that transforms them in a statement like y(t)=T{x(t)}.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagrams or plots are needed; symbolic parsing is sufficient.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}x(\tau)d\tau, identify the correct option for input, output, and system rule.
distractor_plan: Swap x(t) and y(t) roles in at least one option.
Treat the integral operator as the output symbol.
Use a correct-looking expression but assign the same letter to both input and output.
Describe the relation as 'signal equals system' rather than 'system maps input to output.'

paragraph_plan: Identify what the section writer should use: none.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $y(t)=\dfrac{d}{dt}x(t)+2x(t)$, identify the input signal, output signal, and system mapping.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Classify x(t) as input, y(t) as output, and the mapping as a differential linear operator with gain 2.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from a generic definition of system transformation to explicit symbol-level parsing in a nontrivial rule statement.
solution_step_plan: Read the expression and mark every occurrence of independent variable t.
Assign the argument-bearing quantity that is transformed to input.
Assign the left-hand quantity as output.
Name the transformation T{·} implied by the entire right-hand expression.
practice_variation_axes: Different symbolic operators (shift, gain, derivative).
Input/output symbol changes while preserving structure.
Multiple candidate descriptions including decoy system rules.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example and follow-up questions tightly focused on classification, not solving long calculations.

sections.section_title: Applying a Simple System Rule to a Signal
sections.learning_goal: Demonstrate applying a fixed system rule to a concrete input signal without changing the rule.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: Computation is algebraic/substitution-only.

question_policy.practice_question_model: If $T\{x(t)\}=x(t-2)$ and $x(t)=e^{-t}$, which computed signal is the output?
distractor_plan: Incorrectly shift in the wrong direction (t+2 instead of t-2).
Apply input value numerically at one time only instead of as a function.
Multiply where only a shift is intended.
Drop the same symbol (x) and write y(t)=e^{-t}+2.

paragraph_plan: No tutorial-level instructions needed for example section.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Apply $y(t)=x(t-1)$ to $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and simplify the output expression.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the transformed output by substituting $(t-1)$ for t in each input appearance and carrying the same shift through both terms.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds a concrete substitution step to the prior classification of inputs/outputs, while keeping one simple linear time-shift rule.
solution_step_plan: Write the output rule y(t)=x(t-1).
Substitute the given input into every x(·) occurrence.
Track the shift through each term consistently.
State the final y(t) using standard step-function syntax.
practice_variation_axes: Different step-function arguments (delays and advances).
Single-term versus multi-term inputs.
Equivalent algebraic re-expression of the same computed output.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked-example explanation focused on unchanged rule + consistent substitution; practice questions should vary signal form but keep the same rule.

sections.section_title: Recognizing the Same System Rule Across Different Inputs
sections.learning_goal: Train learners to detect a fixed system rule by applying it to multiple input forms and checking rule invariance.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual tasks required; focus on symbolic invariance detection.

question_policy.answer_format: Choice among candidate system-rule statements or selected outputs.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given three mappings, identify which pair of cases use the same underlying rule T{·}: (A) $y(t)=x(t-1)$, (B) $y(t)=x(2t)$, (C) $y(t)=\int x(\tau)d\tau$.
distractor_plan: Treating scaling and shifting as the same rule despite a changed operator.
Overfitting to one specific input form and declaring different rules for equivalent delays.
Ignoring whether integration is present and selecting a shift-only description.

paragraph_plan: No tutorial-style paragraph scaffold is needed in an example section.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x_1(t)=t$, $x_2(t)=e^{-t}$, and $x_3(t)=\sin t$, show how all three follow the same rule $y(t)=x(t-1)+x(t+1)$ and compute one output form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show explicit substitution into the shared rule and confirm no coefficient/operator changes across inputs.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds multiple input families to test transfer of the same rule rather than repeated single-input execution.
solution_step_plan: State the candidate rule once as a shared mapping.
Apply it to each input by replacing t with t−1 and t+1.
Write two outputs explicitly and leave the third in compact form.
Compare results to verify the same transformation structure.
practice_variation_axes: Different input classes (polynomial, exponential, sinusoidal).
Different signed shifts in the same shared rule.
Multiple-choice identification of same-vs-different rule among decoys.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the strongest transfer point for example and question writers; keep distractors rule-focused rather than numeric.

entries.lesson_core_move: Distinguish the input signal, output signal, and transformation direction for a continuous-time system so a situation can be framed as an input-output model before applying system notation and system-property tests.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Inputs and Outputs
sections.learning_goal: State the core distinction between input signal, output signal, and system direction in a basic continuous-time input-output rule.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; all required structure is symbolic and can be introduced with variable mappings only.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define input signal, output signal, and transformation direction as the three-part frame for every continuous-time system statement in this lesson.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Introduce the base case y(t)=x(t), labeling x as input and y as output with direction input→output.
paragraph_plan: Open with a short contrast between a signal and a system rule, then define input, output, and direction in plain terms.
Introduce the standard notation y(t)=T{x(t)} and connect it to the verbal frame: x is fed into the system rule, y is produced.
Show one concrete base case and explicitly test direction by checking whether x appears inside an operator map producing y.
Add one quick rule for verification: choose a physical meaning for x and y only after the system mapping is clear.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section entirely conceptual. No practice questions; do not introduce diagrams. Keep the notation load to one mapping equation and one labeled example before moving to worked examples.

sections.section_title: Identifying Inputs and Outputs from System Descriptions
sections.learning_goal: From a written system description, correctly label the input and output variables.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; learner can identify roles from symbolic form alone.

question_policy.answer_format: identify variable labels as x(t), y(t), or input/output direction
question_policy.practice_question_model: For a system map y(t)=3x(t)+2, identify the input, the output, and the direction of transformation.
distractor_plan: Swap input and output variable roles.
Treat the independent variable t as one of the signals.
Confuse the constant term with input or output.
Reverse direction and claim output drives input.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given y(t)=4x(t)-5, label which quantity is the input signal, which is the output signal, and state the transformation direction.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Build a repeatable method: parse variable placement and determine which signal is being transformed into which.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds a constant term to the base identity form while preserving one-step mapping.
solution_step_plan: Read the equation and identify candidate input and output symbols.
Apply the rule: symbol on left side is output candidate, inside the system argument is input candidate.
State direction input→output and justify with the one-sided dependence shown in y(t)=F(x(t)).
practice_variation_axes: swap symbol names (u/v, a/b, s/r)
change affine forms while preserving structure
add an extra constant gain or offset

sections.handoff_notes: Use short controlled example-to-question transitions. Keep distractors aligned to common role-reversal errors.

sections.section_title: Determining the Direction of a Signal Transformation
sections.learning_goal: Determine whether a given equation implements an input-to-output transform or incorrectly implies the inverse direction.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; direction is inferable from argument structure and variable placement.

question_policy.answer_format: direction judgment and role labeling in one response
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given z(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t} x(\tau)d\tau, which quantity is input and which is output, and what is the transformation direction?
distractor_plan: Read direction from integration bounds instead of dependency form.
Conclude both variables can be inputs simultaneously.
Treat the integration variable as the system output.
Reverse the arrow direction because symbols look similar.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the rule v(t)=\frac{d}{dt}u(t), identify input, output, and direction, and confirm why differentiation indicates a one-way input→output transform.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Anchor direction in explicit dependence: the operator maps one named signal to another, regardless of operator type.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces operator form (derivative/integral) as a controlled wrinkle while keeping one input and one output signal.
solution_step_plan: Identify the output by left-side position.
Identify the mapped signal inside the operator as input.
State direction from mapped signal to left-side signal and avoid interpreting the operator as changing signal identity.
practice_variation_axes: swap differential and integral operators
rename signals while preserving operator type
replace one operator with time scaling

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section focused on direction only; defer formal operator notation depth to later lesson on system notation.

sections.section_title: Assigning Physical Quantities as Input and Output Signals
sections.learning_goal: Select appropriate physical quantities as input and output signals from a system context before coding the rule.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; choices are based on context text and symbolic mapping vocabulary.

question_policy.answer_format: short mapping statement choosing the input/outcome pair
question_policy.practice_question_model: In a temperature-control system where thermostat setting p(t) influences room temperature r(t) through a model block, identify input and output and indicate whether the model maps p(t)→r(t) or r(t)→p(t).
distractor_plan: Choose response variable as input because it is observable.
Label actuator variables and sensor variables backward by convention confusion.
Use unrelated physical quantity not present in description.
Mix up units and treat both signals as outputs simultaneously.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A sensor outputs voltage v_s(t) based on position x(t) through a transfer block. Choose the input and output and phrase the input-output mapping sentence.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Practice physical-to-symbol mapping without changing the underlying mapping rule logic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds physical semantics (sensor/control context) while preserving one-block transformation.
solution_step_plan: Identify which quantity is externally chosen or injected.
Identify which quantity is produced/observed as system response.
Write the sentence: [chosen quantity] is input, [measured quantity] is output, mapping is input→output.
practice_variation_axes: swap physical scenario (mechanical, electrical, thermal)
swap signal names while preserving causal roles
add a unit conversion label without changing direction

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize causal interpretation from context first, notation second. Keep questions short to reduce cognitive load.

sections.section_title: Checking an Input-Output Assignment Against a System Description
sections.learning_goal: Validate whether a proposed input-output pairing is consistent with the stated system rule and reject inconsistent pairings.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagrams are needed; consistency checks are textual and symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: consistency judgment plus corrected input/output labels
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which of the following best matches the system rule y(t)=\int_0^t x(\tau)d\tau: 1) input=x, output=y with input→output; 2) input=y, output=x with input→output; 3) input=x, output=y with output→input; 4) no input/output; 5) both as outputs.
distractor_plan: Pick the option that only mentions equation form but ignores causal role labels.
Accept symmetric phrasing that hides a direction error.
Reject a valid pairing due to operator complexity.
Choose ambiguous answers combining multiple claims.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given a proposed statement 'y is input and x is output' for y(t)=\int_0^t x(\tau)dτ, check and correct the assignment.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Develop a verification checklist that catches swapped roles before moving to notation-intensive topics.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces correction workflow: evaluate a candidate assignment and justify acceptance/rejection.
solution_step_plan: Read proposed assignment as a claim about role labeling.
Compare with the rule structure and identify which signal feeds the operator.
Reject the wrong assignment and replace with the consistent one.
State the corrected direction explicitly in plain language.
practice_variation_axes: swap integrals with derivatives
provide one false and one near-correct distractor pair
change variable names and operator type

sections.handoff_notes: This final example should feel like a quality gate before the lesson ends; include why each wrong option violates the rule.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret continuous-time system notation such as x(t) -> y(t) and y(t) = T{x(t)} by identifying the input signal, system operator, and output signal in an input-output model.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Continuous-Time System Notation
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the core notation for continuous-time systems and connect arrow and operator forms to the same input-output meaning.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual is needed: the notation is read from symbolic expressions.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define a continuous-time system as a transformation from an input signal x(t) to an output signal y(t), read x(t) -> y(t) as direction-sensitive, and define y(t)=T{x(t)} as a function-like operator statement of the same idea.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a single-symbol system rule: from y(t)=2x(t), identify x(t) as input, y(t) as output, and T as scaling by 2.
paragraph_plan: State the naming convention for systems: input, output, and the transformation that connects them.
Introduce arrow notation as the directional map x(t) -> y(t) with y(t) as the system output of x(t).
Introduce operator notation y(t)=T{x(t)} and show it records the same mapping compactly as a rule name.
Show that both notations are interchangeable by translating y(t)=2x(t) to x(t) -> y(t).
Preview the later sections that add controlled twists: identifying inputs/outputs first, then reading T, then translation and naming.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: No worked example or practice questions in this tutorial section; keep the introduction narrow and notation-centric.

sections.section_title: Identifying Input and Output in Arrow Notation
sections.learning_goal: Given arrow-form expressions, correctly assign the input signal symbol and output signal symbol in one direction only.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual object is required; all work is symbol parsing.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a mapping such as x(t) -> 3x(t), identify the input and output symbols and choose the correct pair.
distractor_plan: Swap input/output labels, e.g., treating y(t) as input.
Read the arrow as equality direction reverse.
Add or remove terms in the arrow mapping symbolically.
Confuse x and y when symbols are changed names such as u(t), v(t).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Read this arrow form and identify the input/output: $x(t) \to y(t)=2x(t-1)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Correctly name input x(t) and output y(t), and confirm directional mapping x to y.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Builds from the tutorial base by adding a nontrivial expression on the output side while keeping arrow direction unchanged.
solution_step_plan: Locate the left endpoint of the arrow as input and right endpoint as output.
Confirm that only the arrow direction is used for input-output roles.
Report the input-output pair using explicit words and symbolic labels.
practice_variation_axes: Use shifted time arguments x(t-\tau)
Use alternate symbol names x(t), u(t), v(t)
Use constant gain forms in output expression

sections.handoff_notes: This section locks directionality before operator details are introduced.

sections.section_title: Identifying the System Operator in Operator Notation
sections.learning_goal: From an operator form, identify the rule T and distinguish it from input/output variables.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagram or plot is required for symbolic operator parsing.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given y(t)=T\{u(t)\} where T describes integration, choose the best statement of T.
distractor_plan: Choose the input symbol as the operator name.
Conflate T with the output y(t) instead of the transform rule.
Choose a wrong operator family (differentiation vs multiplication or delay).
Drop the function argument x(t) and answer with only T

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given y(t)=T\{x(t)\} and T\{x(t)\}=x(t-1), identify the operator and restate the system map in operator form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Extract T as the delay-by-1 operator and keep x(t), y(t) roles clear.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds operator extraction to the prior arrow-only parsing by naming the transform rule explicitly.
solution_step_plan: Read the enclosing braces to isolate input argument x(t).
Rewrite T as a concrete rule acting on x(t).
Attach y(t) to that rule to preserve output interpretation.
practice_variation_axes: Use gain operators T\{x\}=k x(t)
Use delay or advance operators T\{x\}=x(t\pm t_0)
Use integral-like shorthand in symbolic form

sections.handoff_notes: Keep operator extraction literal: the learner should never need to compute numeric values here.

sections.section_title: Translating Between Arrow Notation and Operator Notation
sections.learning_goal: Perform one-to-one conversion between x(t) -> y(t) and y(t)=T\{x(t)\} forms.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual is needed because translation is algebraic and symbolic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Convert between equivalent representations: from x(t)\to y(t)=\int_0^t x(\tau)d\tau to operator form and back.
distractor_plan: Swap source and destination notation directions.
Copy the right side into arrow body without naming the operator.
Use wrong transform variable context, e.g., x(t-\tau) where not required.
Drop mapping direction when converting back to arrow notation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Translate this pair exactly and check equivalence: x(t) -> y(t)=\int_0^t x(\tau)d\tau.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the equivalent y(t)=T\{x(t)\} and confirm the same operator-to-map meaning.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Reverses the direction of required conversion, forcing two-way translation after one-way reading in earlier sections.
solution_step_plan: Start from the given notation form.
Identify input, output, and transformation expression.
Rebuild the target notation with the same data and verify semantic equivalence.
practice_variation_axes: Start from operator form and go to arrow form
Swap input/output symbols while preserving role
Use nested symbolic transforms in operator body

sections.handoff_notes: Use explicit equivalence language so example writer can mirror direction checks consistently.

sections.section_title: Interpreting System Notation with Named Signals
sections.learning_goal: Interpret system notation when inputs and outputs use alternate names while preserving role and operator mapping.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual support required; symbol names change only.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given y_0(t)=T\{u(t)\} with T\{u(t)\}=2u(t)-u(t-1), identify input, output, and operator representation as arrow form.
distractor_plan: Treat generic symbols (u, y_0, z) as meaningfully different system equations.
Choose wrong symbol as input due to naming conventions.
Omit braces and rewrite with equality only.
Preserve operator but invert input/output direction.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the operator form y_u(t)=\mathcal{H}\{u(t)\} where \mathcal{H}\{u(t)\}=u(t)^2+1, identify input/output/operator and rewrite in arrow notation.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map named variables to roles correctly and restate the same system in either notation without semantic change.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces alternate symbol conventions and requires abstraction from x,y defaults to reinforce transfer to physical notation.
solution_step_plan: Parse the named input variable and named output variable.
Match the named operator symbol to the same transformation role used earlier.
Write the equivalent arrow notation with new labels.
practice_variation_axes: Swap variable letters and subscripts
Use equivalent operator glyphs like H, S, G
Use additive or gain-based operator bodies

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize symbol renaming as a transfer test; require explicit statement that semantics do not depend on symbols.

entries.lesson_core_move: Map a filter description into continuous-time system notation by identifying the input signal, output signal, and the signal feature the filter passes, attenuates, or modifies.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Filters as Systems
sections.learning_goal: Orient the learner to the filter-as-system viewpoint by naming input/output for filter descriptions and classifying the feature behavior as pass, attenuate, or modify.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual required; the section is handled purely with symbolic descriptions and sentence-level filter language.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define a filter as a system transformation y(t) = T{x(t)} and identify the two roles in any filter description: what signal is accepted as input and what signal is produced as output, then label whether the filter acts by passing, attenuating, or modifying a chosen signal feature.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Introduce a single filter statement (e.g., "low-pass filter reduces high-frequency content") and explicitly mark x(t) as input and y(t) as output.
paragraph_plan: Open with a one-sentence bridge from system notation: all filters are systems, so every filter can be viewed as a map from input signal x(t) to output signal y(t).
State the minimal identification pattern: name the input variable, the output variable, and the key feature behavior in one line of plain notation.
Use a simple worked-in-text example: y(t)=T{x(t)} for a filter that passes low frequencies and attenuates high frequencies, emphasizing feature language first.
Introduce controlled contrast language: passing keeps a feature, attenuating reduces a feature, modifying transforms feature attributes such as gain or delay, and map each into system terminology.
Preview the section sequence: next examples first lock input/output, then each feature class, then full system-notation mapping.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Example placeholder intentionally left empty for tutorial section.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Tutorial-only planning. Do not write section-level exercises or practice. Keep to minimum effective dose before practice-heavy sections.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Input and Output of a Filter
sections.learning_goal: From a filter description, correctly assign input and output signals using a consistent naming convention compatible with system notation.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No diagram is required; signal-function notation is sufficient.

question_policy.answer_format: symbolic signal labels and short sentence labels
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a filter statement, choose the correct ordered input-output pair (x(t) -> y(t)).
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that swaps input and output symbols.
Include a distractor that uses unrelated variable names or a third signal not in the description.
Include a distractor that misidentifies a control/input parameter as the signal.
Include a distractor that gives the correct labels but reverses direction in notation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the filter described as "This filter takes acceleration input a(t) and produces velocity output v(t) by suppressing rapid oscillations", identify x(t) and y(t) in system form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the input-output assignment as y(t) = x(t) map with the filter's variable names relabeled consistently.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses text from the tutorial base case but adds explicit variable names and a behavior clause to force careful extraction.
solution_step_plan: Extract the signal receiving energy from source as the input candidate.
Identify the returned signal as the output candidate.
Check dimensions/roles (source/excitation vs response) to remove ambiguity.
Write the assignment in the standardized form y(t)=T{x(t)}.
practice_variation_axes: input/output variable naming order
whether statement is causal language-based or equation-based
signal domain tags (time-domain vs sampled/other notation)

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this example tightly focused on role assignment; do not also test feature classification yet.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Signal Feature a Filter Passes
sections.learning_goal: Classify a filter as passing a signal feature and distinguish it from attenuation or modification using filter language plus minimal symbolic cues.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No plots needed; this section remains linguistic and symbolic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose which signal feature (low-frequency band, DC component, amplitude component, or edge content) the described filter passes.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that confuses pass behavior with attenuation behavior.
Include a distractor that names the output equation modifier instead of feature.
Include a distractor that misclassifies the pass feature by frequency band.
Include a distractor that uses phase-shift wording for a magnitude-only filter.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A filter states: "This filter keeps DC and low-frequency components and reduces rapid oscillations." Identify the feature it passes in system terms.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: State that the feature passed is the low-frequency / near-DC content and label it explicitly as the pass behavior of T\{x(t)\}.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from labeling x/y to classifying a specific feature while using the same two-signal mapping pattern.
solution_step_plan: Read the feature phrase and isolate the preserved component.
Map that preserved component to pass behavior.
Attach it to the filter rule without changing the input-output form.
Use a concise phrase suitable for downstream explanation: "This system passes ..."
practice_variation_axes: frequency-band keywords
time-domain feature wording (DC vs ripple/edges)
single-feature versus mixed-feature descriptions

sections.handoff_notes: Do not require computations; this is classification by semantic feature extraction only.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Signal Feature a Filter Attenuates
sections.learning_goal: Identify the filter feature that is reduced in strength while distinguishing attenuation from mere omission or complete blocking.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; include attenuation language in statements.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose which signal feature is attenuated by the described filter and avoid classifying weakened gain as complete removal.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that labels attenuation as passing.
Include a distractor that uses an unrelated feature from a different domain (e.g., phase vs magnitude).
Include a distractor that mistakes complete block for attenuation.
Include a distractor that inverts the described feature direction.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A filter says: "This filter reduces the energy of high-frequency components and suppresses fast fluctuations." Identify the feature it attenuates.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify the attenuated feature as the high-frequency/rapid fluctuation component and phrase it as a reduction, not elimination.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Shifts from pass-classification to attenuation-classification using parallel wording and same extraction routine.
solution_step_plan: Parse action verbs and isolate the weakened output property.
Map that property into a named feature class (e.g., high-frequency attenuation).
Confirm it is not complete blocking or inversion.
Return concise filter behavior sentence linked to system role.
practice_variation_axes: attenuated feature strength (strong/partial)
feature domain (frequency, smoothness, amplitude envelope)
signal feature phrasing overlap with pass section

sections.handoff_notes: This section sets contrast with pass-type behavior; keep answer choices short to reinforce category distinctions.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Signal Feature a Filter Modifies
sections.learning_goal: Select the signal feature that the filter changes in kind (gain, phase, delay, shape) rather than only passing or suppressing it.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual needed.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the modified characteristic (e.g., phase, gain, delay) from a filter description with explicit transformation language.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that confuses modification with attenuation.
